analysis.investment_thesis: Alok Industries is a technically insolvent textile company with negative equity of INR 21,527 Cr, revenue declining at -9% CAGR over 9 years, and persistent net losses — there is no growth story here, only a zombie balance sheet. At EV/EBITDA of 320x on razor-thin and volatile EBITDA, the market is pricing in a turnaround that has repeatedly failed to materialize.
key_strengths: Reliance Industries as promoter (75%) provides implicit backstop against outright liquidation
Gross margin of 31.5% shows the underlying textile operations retain some pricing power
OCF was positive 4 of last 5 years, including INR 419 Cr in FY26, meaning the business generates some operating cash
key_risks: Catastrophically insolvent balance sheet: negative equity of INR 21,527 Cr against borrowings of INR 26,106 Cr — debt is 7x annual revenue
Revenue in structural decline — FY26 revenue of INR 3,715 Cr is less than half FY17's INR 8,723 Cr, with no recovery trend
Finance costs of INR 615 Cr exceed EBITDA of INR 291 Cr in FY26 — the company cannot service its debt from operations
red_flags: Negative book value: equity of -INR 21,527 Cr makes P/B meaningless at -0.33
Seven consecutive years of net losses; the only 'profits' in 2019-2020 were debt write-off accounting gains (Other Income of INR 7,063 Cr and INR 2,082 Cr)
EV/EBITDA of 320x is not a growth premium — it reflects a balance sheet so debt-laden that even minimal EBITDA produces an absurd multiple
Revenue contracted from INR 7,310 Cr (FY22) to INR 3,715 Cr (FY26) — a 49% decline in 4 years — while losses persist
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Alok Industries is precisely the kind of stock Peter Lynch would warn investors away from: a "turnaround" that has been turning around for over a decade and never arrived. The company entered insolvency proceedings in 2020, was taken over by Reliance/JM Financial, and yet sits today with negative equity of INR 21,527 Cr and borrowings of INR 26,106 Cr — a debt pile 7x its annual revenue of INR 3,715 Cr. Finance costs alone (INR 615 Cr) exceed full-year EBITDA (INR 291 Cr), meaning the business cannot even cover interest from operations. The "Other Income" windfalls of INR 7,063 Cr (FY19) and INR 2,082 Cr (FY20) were debt haircuts, not business performance — and even those couldn't arrest the spiral.

There is no Lynch-style "story" here. Revenue has declined at -9% CAGR over nine years with no sign of reversal. Operating margins oscillate around zero (-4.51% currently). The EV/EBITDA of 320x is not a premium for growth — it is a distortion caused by a balance sheet carrying INR 26,106 Cr in debt against a market cap of only INR 7,095 Cr. The stock trades as a speculative option on Reliance eventually engineering a rescue, not on business fundamentals. For a GARP investor, there is no growth to price, no reasonable price to pay, and no margin of safety whatsoever.
